🔊 Leveraging immense potential of people key to realizing stronger Iran: IRGC chief

📌 Tehran, IRNA — Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) Major General Ahmad Vahidi, says realizing a "stronger Iran" depends on harnessing the immense capacity of the people and their  “Basiji” spirit.

In a message, marking the anniversary of the establishment of the Basij Organization on Thursday, General Vahidi described the foundation of Basij-e Mostaz’afin (Mobilization of the Oppressed) — a volunteer forces organization — as a far-sighted and strategic initiative of the founder of the Islamic Republic, Imam Khomeini.
​
Quoting this year’s Basij Week theme, “Basij: Devoted to the People, Hope for the Underprivileged,” the IRGC chief called the occasion a valuable opportunity to renew pledges to the ideals of the late Imam, the martyred leader of the Islamic Revolution, and other esteemed martyrs.
​
Praising and honoring the volunteer forces’ sincere, selfless efforts across various arenas, he remembered their valuable roles during the era of the Eight-Year Sacred Defense (Iraqi invasion of war) and in confronting various seditions and threats over the past few decades.
​
Through their steadfastness and collaboration with the Armed Forces, members of Basij added further golden chapters to their glorious record, especially during the war imposed by the American-Israeli enemy and its regional and extra-regional backers and allies, Vahidi said.
​
Stating that a stronger and progressive Iran requires harnessing the immense potential of the people, he underscored that the Basij — grounded in faith and operating through a neighborhood-centered approach — would keep countering the hybrid threats of global hegemony and Zionism and safeguarding national security.
​
The top IRGC commander reiterated his warning that any act of aggression against Iran’s security and territorial integrity will be met with an immediate, crushing response from the military and Basiji forces.
​
He further extended his congratulations on the occasion to all Basij members, the families of martyrs and veterans, as well as the commanders and officials of the Basij across the country.
​
“I hope that by preserving the revolutionary spirit, enhancing comprehensive readiness, safeguarding the legacy of the two late leaders of the Islamic Revolution, and by following the guidelines of Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei and relying on the slogan ‘Every Iranian, one Basiji,’ we shall witness the further consolidation of national unity,” General Vahidi concluded his message.

The Baltic Powder Keg 🌍⚠️: Secret Diplomacy Aims to Prevent a Russia-NATO Clash


The Baltic Sea is becoming one of the most dangerous potential flashpoints between Russia and the West. Behind the scenes, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre have reportedly pursued an unusual diplomatic effort to prevent tensions from escalating into a direct military confrontation with Moscow.

According to The Wall Street Journal, the two leaders used a conversation with Putin on October 27 to deliver a message: NATO had no intention of imposing a naval blockade in the Baltic Sea.

The stakes are high. More than 60% of Russia's seaborne oil exports pass through the region, making it a vital economic artery for Moscow. Meanwhile, Russian warships have increasingly escorted commercial tankers, including vessels linked to the so-called shadow fleet used to circumvent Western sanctions. 

Germany's coast guard reportedly recorded around 260 such military escorts in the Baltic and North Sea over just over a year.

Several maritime incidents have heightened fears of escalation. In June, a Russian warship confronted German coast guard vessels after Greenpeace activists approached a tanker suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet. German officials described the encounter as carrying a significant risk of confrontation.

Political statements have further complicated the situation. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski called for NATO military exercises near Kaliningrad, while Estonia's foreign minister discussed the possibility of closing the Gulf of Finland. According to the WSJ, Pentagon officials urged Baltic counterparts to avoid rhetoric that could provoke Moscow.

Concerned that Western assurances were not reaching the Kremlin, Stubb reportedly helped establish an indirect channel through a Russian oligarch with access to Putin. The intermediary traveled to Norway for consultations before carrying the message to Moscow.

During their subsequent conversation, Stubb emphasized that Finland had no intention of blocking the Baltic in peacetime and would respect international maritime law. Putin welcomed the contact but warned that Russia would respond to any attempt to challenge its interests.

The diplomatic effort faces new challenges. Ukrainian drones recently struck a Russian cargo vessel near Finland. Finnish authorities coordinated rescue operations with Russia, while Zelensky said the ship was a legitimate target because it was carrying weapons.

The incidents illustrate how commercial shipping, sanctions enforcement and military security are increasingly intertwined in the Baltic. European governments now face a delicate balancing act: maintaining pressure on Russia while preventing a miscalculation that could trigger a direct confrontation between Moscow and NATO.
